claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations.
The hierarchical heterostructure of HfNbTiVAl10 has been confirmed by electron microscopy.
High-resolution microscopy can provide representative volume elements that capture the relevant multiscale heterogeneity of HfNbTiVAl10.
Reduced-order finite-element simulations on image-derived RVEs can generate useful local stress-strain fields.
Reduced-order finite-element simulations can provide cues for fracture initiation from the detailed microstructure.
Local phase morphology, gradient fluctuations, and interfacial area are representative descriptors of the hierarchical microstructure.
Embedding finite-element outputs and microstructural descriptors in a physics-constrained machine-learning model can bridge mesoscale behavior to macroscopic mechanical properties.
Uncertainty quantification and an expanded calibration dataset will improve the reliability of the surrogate model.
The surrogate model can predict Young's modulus of hierarchical-heterostructured HfNbTiVAl10 under room-temperature quasi-static tensile testing.
The surrogate model can predict yield strength of hierarchical-heterostructured HfNbTiVAl10 under room-temperature quasi-static tensile testing.
The surrogate model can predict fracture toughness of hierarchical-heterostructured HfNbTiVAl10.
Predictions of Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness are expected to be within ±5–10% of experimental measurements.
The proposed approach is expected to be approximately 10 times faster than traditional CALPHAD, first-principles, or full-field simulation methods.

The proposed approach will improve predictive accuracy relative to conventional thermophysical-parameter calculations, CALPHAD, first-principles simulations, and machine-learning models lacking integrated microstructural inputs.
Model reliability may degrade for microstructures outside the variability represented in the training data.
Model reliability may degrade at high strain rates or temperatures substantially different from room temperature.
Model generalizability is sensitive to the quality and size of the training dataset.
